did_you_know.text: Did you know? Amos’s prophecy in this chapter is addressed to the entire family of Israel and reminds them that the Lord brought them up from Egypt.
Did you know? Precisely because the Lord knew and chose Israel more than any other family on earth, he will also punish them for their sins; closeness brings responsibility.
Did you know? The question “Do two walk together unless they have agreed to do so?” begins a series of rhetorical questions emphasizing that events do not happen without a connection or cause.
Did you know? Amos compares the blowing of the trumpet in a city to a warning that strikes fear into the people, and presents calamity in the city as part of the Lord’s judgment.
Did you know? According to the chapter, the Lord reveals his secret to his servants the prophets before he does what they warn about.
Did you know? Just as a lion’s roar inspires fear, the word of the Lord moves the prophet to speak and prophesy; prophecy is presented as a response to hearing God’s word.
Did you know? Ashdod and Egypt are called to gather and observe the turmoil and oppression in Samaria, as though the injustice were being openly displayed as a witness before other nations.
Did you know? The people of Samaria are described as those who do not know how to do what is right, while in their palaces they store up violence and robbery.
Did you know? Amos uses the image of a shepherd rescuing from a lion only two legs or a piece of an ear to describe how few of the Israelites living in Samaria will escape.
Did you know? The punishment in this chapter is not limited to the altars of Bethel; the luxurious winter houses, summer houses, and ivory houses will also be destroyed.
